• Building effective agents (Anthropic engineering)

column2:
Your research system reviews vendor contracts across four independent dimensions: data privacy, liability, pricing terms, and termination clauses. A single prompt covering all four misses about 25% of issues in whichever dimensions appear last in the instructions, and reviewers need results within roughly one call's latency, not four calls' worth.

Which structure fixes the missed issues while respecting the latency constraint?

A. Sectioning: run four parallel calls, one per dimension, and aggregate the findings.
B. A chained sequence of four calls, one dimension at a time, carrying findings forward.
C. One call to a larger model with the four dimensions restated at both ends of the prompt.
D. Voting: run the same full four-dimension review three times in parallel and merge the issues found.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is the sectioning form of parallelization: the four dimensions are independent subtasks, so each gets its own focused call — eliminating the attention-driven misses on later dimensions — while wall-clock time stays near a single call because they run simultaneously. Option B fixes the focus problem but stacks four calls of sequential latency, exactly what the requirement rules out. Option C is the bigger-model-and-more-emphasis fix for a structural attention problem; one overloaded prompt still juggles four analyses. Option D reruns the same overloaded prompt, and voting averages out random error but not systematic error — every run shares the same bias toward neglecting the later dimensions.

column2:
A code-review step flags insecure database queries before merge. A single Claude review call catches an injected test vulnerability in only 80% of runs, and the misses look random rather than systematic. The security team wants detection above 95% while keeping review time near a single call's latency.

Which change best raises detection?

A. Have the reviewer output a confidence score per file and re-review any file scored below 0.7.
B. Set the temperature to 0 so the reviewer behaves identically on every run of the same diff.
C. Run several review calls in parallel on the same diff and flag anything that any run flags.
D. Chain three sequential review passes, each one starting from the previous pass's findings.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is the voting form of parallelization: multiple independent attempts at the same task whose outputs are aggregated — if each run catches a miss-at-random vulnerability 80% of the time, taking the union across several parallel runs pushes detection far past 95% while latency stays near one call because the runs execute simultaneously. Option A gates re-review on self-reported confidence, a signal that correlates poorly with what the model actually missed. Option B makes results repeatable — including repeatable misses; determinism adds no recall. Option D triples latency and biases later passes toward confirming what earlier passes found instead of looking independently.

column2:
Your multi-agent research system pipes every query through a fixed pipeline: one search subagent, one analysis subagent, and one synthesis subagent, each run exactly once. Simple lookups waste two stages, while multi-domain questions — 'compare the last three years of privacy rulings across two jurisdictions' — fail because the number and type of searches required cannot be known until the query itself is examined.

Which pattern fits this variability?

A. Extend the fixed pipeline to five stages so complex queries receive more search and analysis processing.
B. Orchestrator-workers: a lead model examines each query, delegates the subtasks it decides are needed to workers, and synthesizes the results.
C. Routing: classify queries as simple, medium, or complex and send each class to one of three fixed pipelines sized for it.
D. Evaluator-optimizer: keep the current pipeline but loop the synthesis stage until an evaluator approves the answer.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B matches the defining trigger for orchestrator-workers: subtasks that cannot be predicted in advance. The orchestrator dynamically decomposes each query, spawns however many search or analysis workers that particular question needs, and synthesizes their results — one search for a lookup, six for a cross-jurisdiction comparison. Option A keeps a predefined decomposition, just a longer one: still wasteful for lookups and still the wrong shape for novel query structures. Option C reduces the waste but each bucket still hides unbounded variety — a 'complex' pipeline is still a fixed pipeline. Option D iterates on synthesis quality when the failure happens upstream: the wrong set of searches was run in the first place, and no amount of re-synthesis recovers missing research.

column2:
Your synthesis subagent drafts research summaries that must satisfy a 10-point editorial rubric. Single-pass drafts fail the rubric 40% of the time even though the rubric is already included in the generation prompt. Separately, you have verified that a Claude call given a draft plus the rubric identifies the specific failing points with high agreement against human editors.

Which pattern best exploits that verified grading ability?

A. Generate five independent drafts in parallel and publish whichever one the grader ranks best.
B. Append the grader's rubric a second time at the end of the generation prompt so it gets more emphasis.
C. Have the drafting model grade its own output and revise until it awards itself a passing score.
D. Loop draft, grade, revise, feeding the grader's critique back to the drafter until the rubric passes or an attempt cap is hit.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is the evaluator-optimizer pattern — a generator and a distinct evaluator in a feedback loop — and it fits precisely because the two preconditions hold: clear evaluation criteria exist, and iterative refinement demonstrably adds value since the grader pinpoints the exact failing rubric points for the drafter to fix. Option A pays for five full drafts while discarding the grader's most valuable output, its specific critique; selection without refinement can leave you publishing the least-bad failure. Option B is repetition of instructions already present — the prompt-only approach that produced the 40% failure rate. Option C collapses the roles: self-grading is exactly the unreliable self-assessment the verified independent grader exists to replace.

column2:
Your deployment agent edits YAML service configs with a text-editing tool and then reports success. In 12% of runs the resulting file is invalid — an edit landed inside the wrong block, or the file had been changed by another process since the agent last saw it — yet the transcript shows the agent confidently reporting success anyway.

Which TWO changes most improve the agent's reliability? (Select TWO.)

A. Add a system-prompt instruction telling the agent to be extremely careful with YAML structure and indentation.
B. Have the agent re-read the file immediately before editing so its edits apply to the current state.
C. Set the temperature of the editing calls to 0 so the same edit is produced on every run.
D. After each edit, have the agent re-read or lint the file and treat any failure as feedback to fix before reporting success.
column3:
Correct Answer: B and D. Options B and D are environment inspection applied before and after action: an agent cannot assume the effect of its actions, so reading current state before editing eliminates the stale-file failures, and validating after editing converts silent corruption into feedback the agent can act on in-loop — fixing the wrong-block edits instead of reporting success over a broken file. Option A changes no observation the agent makes; a carefully worded prompt still leaves the agent blind to the file's actual state, so the same failures recur politely. Option C addresses randomness, but the failures stem from unobserved state, not variance — a deterministic edit against a stale or misread file is deterministically wrong.

column2:
You are building an assistant for internal developer requests: 'find why this test is flaky,' 'upgrade this dependency and fix the breakage,' 'trace where this config value comes from.' After mapping 40 sample tickets you cannot write a step sequence that covers even half of them — yet all were solvable using file search, file reading, and command execution.

Which architecture fits this workload?

A. An agent that plans its own steps per request, looping over a small set of general tools — search, read, execute — until done.
B. A routing workflow that classifies each request into one of the 40 mapped types and runs that type's scripted steps.
C. A chained workflow containing the union of all steps observed across the 40 tickets, executed in a fixed order.
D. A parallelization workflow that runs every candidate step simultaneously and aggregates whichever ones succeed.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is the situation agents exist for: when required steps cannot be predetermined, the model plans dynamically, observes the environment after each action, and composes a small flexible toolset in ways you never enumerated — and the stem confirms the whole workload reduces to a few general capabilities. Option B scripts the past; the mapping already failed to cover half of the observed tickets, and novel request shapes keep arriving. Option C executes mostly irrelevant steps on every request and still breaks the moment a ticket needs an unobserved sequence. Option D parallelizes steps that are inherently dependent — you must find the flaky test before you can fix it — so running everything at once is incoherent for these tasks.

column2:
Your document-processing agent has 22 hyper-specific tools (extract_invoice_date, extract_invoice_total, extract_po_number, and so on). Every new document type triggers a request for three or four more tools, requests that match no existing tool simply fail, and the tool list already consumes 3,500 prompt tokens.

How should the toolset be redesigned?

A. Keep the 22 specialized tools but write richer descriptions so the agent selects the correct one more often.
B. Merge all 22 tools into one extract_field tool whose operation enum lists every supported field.
C. Replace them with a few general, composable tools — for example a document reader plus code execution — that the agent combines per request.
D. Add a second routing model that inspects each request and pre-selects which specialized tool the agent may call.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C applies the tool-abstraction principle: agents work best with a small set of general tools they can combine in unanticipated ways — the same reason Claude Code ships with bash and file tools rather than a refactor_tool — so generic read-and-compute capabilities cover novel document types without minting a new tool per field. Option A improves selection among existing tools, but the observed failures are coverage gaps — requests with no matching tool — which no description can close. Option B compresses the list without adding capability; the enum still enumerates fields, so novel fields still fail. Option D is an over-engineered routing layer that spends effort choosing among tools that collectively still cannot do the job.
